design_detail: Secondary analysis of four independent cross-sectional US household surveys (National Household Surveys on Drug Abuse 1991, 1992, 1993 and the 1994a subsample that kept the old questions), pooled. Ages (whole years) of first alcohol or tobacco use, of the first chance to try marijuana and cocaine, and of first use of each, all recalled at interview, were rearranged into person-year records. Discrete-time survival methods: unadjusted cumulative probability curves (Figs. 1–2), and survival regressions within risk sets defined by census tract or city block group and survey year, with sex, race/ethnicity and age group as covariates and earlier drug use as a time-varying exposure, giving relative risks of (a) a first opportunity and (b) first use once an opportunity had occurred. A supplementary analysis drops people whose first use fell in the same year as their first opportunity ('rapid transition') as a check on active drug-seeking. Marijuana analyses use ages 12–18 (n=26,015); cocaine analyses ages 12–25 (n=44,624).
can_establish: That among US household residents aged 12–25 interviewed in 1991–94, those who reported earlier alcohol or tobacco use also reported an earlier first chance to try marijuana and more often started it once they had the chance, and that reported marijuana use went with an earlier first chance to try cocaine and with starting cocaine once offered, after conditioning on neighbourhood, survey year, sex, race/ethnicity and age group.
cannot_establish: That earlier drug use causes later opportunities or later use: no individual propensity (temperament, conduct problems, family or peer drug use) was measured, the timing comes from ages recalled in whole years with same-year events of uncertain order, and the opportunity itself is a self-defined, recalled event that was not validated.

sample.recruitment: Household survey: multistage area-probability samples of the US noninstitutionalized civilian population; persons with no fixed address, institutionalized persons and military personnel are outside the frame; response rates 84.2% (1991), 82.5% (1992), 79.2% (1993) and 85.3% (1994) (p. 919, Materials and Methods, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ages 12–18 for marijuana analyses (n=8,976, 8,179, 7,617 and 1,243 by survey year) and 12–25 for cocaine analyses (n=15,546, 14,766, 12,338 and 1,974); 1994 data from the 1994a subsample asked the old questions on opportunity (p. 919, Materials and Methods, 2nd–3rd paragraphs). Exclusions for missing answers are not described.
sample.demographics: Marijuana sample (Table 1): 13,044 male and 12,971 female; 11,463 non-Hispanic White, 6,798 non-Hispanic Black, 6,290 Hispanic, 1,016 Asian/Pacific Islander and 448 American Indian; 11,641 aged 12–14, 3,760 aged 15 and 10,614 aged 16–18; 49% had used alcohol or tobacco and 14% marijuana (editors' calculation). Cocaine sample (Table 2): 21,297 male and 23,327 female; 18,708 aged 19–25; 27% had used marijuana and 8.1% cocaine (editors' calculation) (p. 921).
sample.selection_effects: Household samples miss people without a fixed address, in institutions or in the military, and people who died young; the authors argue that including the most heavily involved would strengthen the associations (p. 923, Discussion, 2nd paragraph). No use of sampling weights is described, so the estimates describe the respondents rather than the weighted US population.

exposure.measurement: Standardized self-report (interview or questionnaire with procedures to encourage complete and accurate reporting): ages at first use of alcohol, tobacco, marijuana and cocaine, even once; alcohol/tobacco onset is the earlier of the two; there was no question on the first opportunity to try alcohol or tobacco (p. 919, Materials and Methods, 4th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol and tobacco combined into one onset variable; cocaine opportunity analyses stratified by alcohol/tobacco history and marijuana history; other drugs were not considered.

comparison.controls: Respondents in the same risk set (census tract or block group and survey year) who had not yet used the earlier drug at each year of age, earlier use being coded 0 until the event and 1 afterwards (p. 919, Materials and Methods, 7th paragraph; p. 920, 8th paragraph).
comparison.matching: Conditioning on neighbourhood and survey year by stratified risk sets, plus covariate adjustment for sex, race/ethnicity and age group at interview; for cocaine, also age at first marijuana use (pp. 919–920, Materials and Methods, 4th, 7th and 8th paragraphs).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No individual measures of propensity: temperament, conduct or school problems, family drug use and peer drug use were not included. The neighbourhood strata address area-level availability, policing and disorder only.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: For marijuana outcomes the comparison is people who had not used alcohol or tobacco by that age; for cocaine outcomes, people who had not used marijuana, within strata of alcohol/tobacco history.

outcomes.instruments: Self-reported age at the first chance to try marijuana and cocaine (if the respondent had wanted to) and at first use of each, in whole years (p. 919, Materials and Methods, 4th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation of the opportunity questions is reported; the authors note there is no gold standard for either age (p. 923, Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Opportunity = reported age of the first chance; transition = first use at or after the opportunity; 'rapid transition' = first use within the same year as the first opportunity (difference under 1 year), excluded in the drug-seeking check (p. 920, Materials and Methods, 9th paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; most reported p values are below 0.001.

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted relative risks from discrete-time survival regression: first chance to try marijuana, alcohol/tobacco use against none, about 3 (95% CI 2.8 to 3.3); starting marijuana once offered, about 7 (5.7 to 9.5), and 8.9 (5.7 to 14.1) after excluding same-year transitions; first chance to try cocaine against people who had used none of the three, 1.9 (1.7 to 2.1) after alcohol or tobacco only, 4.6 (3.8 to 5.6) after marijuana only and 7.6 (6.9 to 8.4) after both; starting cocaine once offered, marijuana against none, 15 (11.3 to 19.8), and 20.4 (10.2 to 40.7) after excluding same-year transitions (pp. 920, 923). Cumulative probabilities (unadjusted curves): a chance to try marijuana by 18 for about three in four people who had used alcohol or tobacco against one in four of others (text; about 70% and 25% on Fig. 1A); a chance to try cocaine by 25 of 13%, 26%, 51% and 75% across the four alcohol/tobacco and marijuana groups. Crude lifetime odds ratios in Tables 1–2 (63.8 for marijuana after alcohol or tobacco; 100.8 for cocaine after marijuana) are not time-ordered.
analysis.covariates: Sex, race/ethnicity, age group at interview and survey year; risk sets defined by census tract or block group; for cocaine, age at first marijuana use and strata of alcohol/tobacco history.
analysis.selective_reporting: Per-survey estimates are said to be essentially comparable but are in appendix tables available on request or on a website (not read). Several relative risks are printed only as approximate multiples (about three, about seven, 15), and whether each is adjusted is not always stated.
analysis.power: Not reported; the samples are large, but the transition analyses are restricted to people who reported an opportunity, and the number of people without earlier drug use who had an opportunity is not given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In US household residents aged 12–25 (1991–94), reported earlier use of alcohol or tobacco went with about a threefold higher rate of a first chance to try marijuana and, once offered, about a sevenfold higher rate of starting it; reported marijuana use went with 4.6- to 7.6-fold higher rates of a first chance to try cocaine and, once offered, a 15-fold higher rate of starting it. Both transition associations held (8.9 and 20.4) when same-year transitions were dropped. All rest on ages recalled in whole years, conditioning on neighbourhood, survey year, sex, race/ethnicity and age group, with no measure of individual propensity.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion presents the results as new evidence on a possibly causal association and as the first epidemiologic support for two separate mechanisms, one acting on opportunity and one on use once offered (p. 923, Discussion, 1st paragraph), and speculates, labelled as such, that parental supervision works by reducing opportunities (p. 924, 7th paragraph). The data locate the associations at two points in the sequence; they do not show why they arise, and a shared individual propensity would produce both. The abstract's statement that the associations did not arise solely from drug-seeking rests on dropping same-year transitions, which removed 73% of people who used cocaine and, as the authors note, also people who took up an unbidden offer at once under peer pressure (p. 923; p. 924, Discussion, 5th paragraph). The text's three in four by age 18 is about 70% on Fig. 1A.

timeline.event: Kandel: stages of adolescent drug involvement, the sequence these analyses elaborate (see that card).
This study: four US household surveys, 1991–94.

Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: a model calibrated to US household surveys of 1982–94 (overlapping these data) in which a shared propensity and the order of first opportunities, with no gateway effect, reproduce the gateway phenomena (see that card).
Lynskey et al.: within Australian twin pairs, early cannabis use went with later other drug use; access to other drugs through cannabis contacts is among the mechanisms they propose (see that card).
Degenhardt et al., 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys: the order of first use varied with how common each drug was (as recorded on that card).

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no independent replication of the opportunity analyses appears in the sources read for this card; the authors build on their group's earlier analyses of US and Panamanian surveys (references 11–15, not read). Morral et al. (2002) used overlapping US survey data to show that a shared propensity together with the order of opportunities can reproduce the gateway pattern, which fits these results but does not distinguish a causal from a shared-liability explanation. Later studies were not searched by this reader.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Drug Abuse R01 award (grants DA 09897 and DA 09897-04S2) and Mexico's National Council on Science and Technology (CONACyT) (scholarship 110421 and repatriation grant 000358) (Acknowledgments, p. 924).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Bloomberg School of Public Health, Johns Hopkins University; the first author also at the Instituto Nacional de Psiquiatría, Mexico (p. 918).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that records offers and first use as they happen (in months rather than recalled years), measures individual propensity before any use, and compares people who reach a first opportunity for a later drug with and without prior use of the earlier one; ideally with variation in opportunity that does not depend on the person, such as changes in local availability.

domains.note: Neighbourhood (census tract or block group), survey year, sex, race/ethnicity and age group were conditioned on, but no individual propensity (temperament, conduct problems, family or peer drug use) was measured, and such factors plausibly drive both earlier use and later opportunities and use.
Ages of first alcohol, tobacco and marijuana use recalled in whole years by people aged 12–25; events in the same year have an unknown order and were handled by censoring at the tie.
Household frame without homeless, institutionalized or military people; response 79–85%; no sampling weights described.
Exclusions for missing answers and the number of people censored at tied events are not reported; the counts of 12–18-year-olds differ between Tables 1 and 2 (see reporting issues).

The opportunity is a self-defined, recalled event without validation; people who used an earlier drug may notice, define and remember offers differently from people who did not, in a direction that cannot be predicted.
Per-survey results are only in appendix tables not published with the article; several estimates are printed as approximate multiples without stating the model.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The analysis adds a step that stage studies lacked (whether an earlier drug goes with being offered the next one, or with accepting it once offered) and conditions on neighbourhood, but it rests on recalled whole-year ages and has no measure of individual propensity, so it cannot separate an effect of prior use from a shared liability. Citable for the conditional rates and adjusted relative risks as associations in US household residents aged 12–25 in 1991–94, and for the finding that the associations persisted when same-year transitions were excluded; not as evidence that alcohol, tobacco or marijuana use causes later opportunities or later use.

key_findings.finding: Four independent US household surveys (1991, 1992, 1993 and the 1994a subsample) with response rates of 84.2%, 82.5%, 79.2% and 85.3%; marijuana analyses used 26,015 respondents aged 12–18 (8,976, 8,179, 7,617 and 1,243) and cocaine analyses 44,624 aged 12–25 (15,546, 14,766, 12,338 and 1,974).

Respondents reported, in whole years, the age at first use of each drug and the age at which they first had a chance to try marijuana or cocaine had they wanted to; no opportunity question was asked for alcohol or tobacco. Events reported at the same age had an uncertain order; such respondents contributed person-years only up to the year of the tie.

Relative risks came from discrete-time survival regression within risk sets defined by census tract or city block group and survey year, meant to limit confounding by neighbourhood drug availability, police presence and disorder, adjusted for sex, race/ethnicity and age group, with earlier drug use and opportunity coded as time-varying. As a check on drug-seeking, people whose first use came in the same year as their first opportunity were excluded.

By age 18, an estimated three in four people who had used alcohol or tobacco had had a chance to try marijuana, against one in four of those who had not; adjusted relative risk of a first marijuana opportunity about 3 (95% CI 2.8 to 3.3), with comparable estimates in the four surveys (appendix tables not published with the article).
key_findings.locator: Results › Accounting for the opportunity to try marijuana, 1st paragraph (p. 920); Fig. 1, part A (p. 922)
key_findings.note: On a 300-dpi crop of Fig. 1A, the curve for people who had used alcohol or tobacco ends at about 70% at age 18 and the other at about 25% (first reader's reading); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Once offered marijuana, an estimated 85–90% of people who had used alcohol or tobacco started using it, with a median lag of 1 year, against under 25% within 6 years (under 20% within 5 years) of those who had used neither.
key_findings.locator: Results › Marijuana use, given a marijuana exposure opportunity, 1st paragraph (p. 920); Fig. 1, part B (p. 922)
key_findings.note: The 85–90% has no stated time horizon; on Fig. 1B the curve is about 88% at 5 years and approaches 100% by about 13 years, the long tail resting on few people (first reader's reading).

key_findings.finding: Survival regression: people who had used alcohol or tobacco were about seven times as likely to start marijuana once offered (95% CI 5.7 to 9.5), in pooled data and in each survey; excluding same-year transitions, adjusted relative risk 8.9 (95% CI 5.7 to 14.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Marijuana use, given a marijuana exposure opportunity, 2nd paragraph; Results › Do these observed findings depend on seeking out marijuana exposure?, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Estimated cumulative probability of a chance to try cocaine by age 25: 13% in people who had used no alcohol, tobacco or marijuana; 26% after alcohol or tobacco without marijuana; 51% after marijuana without alcohol or tobacco; 75% after marijuana and alcohol or tobacco. Median age at first cocaine opportunity 17 after marijuana with alcohol or tobacco, against 23 after marijuana without them. The association with alcohol/tobacco history differed across strata (chi-square 10.89, 1 df, p<0.001), so analyses were stratified.
key_findings.locator: Results › From marijuana use to cocaine exposure opportunity, 1st paragraph (p. 920) and 2nd paragraph (begins p. 920, continues between the tables on p. 921 and on p. 923); Fig. 2, part A (p. 922)

key_findings.finding: Adjusted relative risk of a first chance to try cocaine, against people who had used none of the three: 1.9 (95% CI 1.7 to 2.1) after alcohol or tobacco without marijuana; 4.6 (3.8 to 5.6) after marijuana without alcohol or tobacco; 7.6 (6.9 to 8.4) after both.
key_findings.locator: Results › From marijuana use to cocaine exposure opportunity, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Once offered cocaine, an estimated 50% of people who had used marijuana started within 2 years, and most eventually did; for people who had not used marijuana the estimates were small at 2 years and under 10% many years later. Relative risk 15 (95% CI 11.3 to 19.8); the association did not differ by alcohol/tobacco history (chi-square 1.77, 1 df, p>0.18).
key_findings.locator: Results › From marijuana use to cocaine use, given a cocaine exposure opportunity, 1st paragraph (p. 923); Fig. 2, part B (p. 922)
key_findings.note: On Fig. 2B (adjusted for alcohol/tobacco use) the curve for people who had used marijuana is about 55% at 2 years and levels off near 75% (first reader's reading).

key_findings.finding: 73% of people who used cocaine reported first use at the same age as their first cocaine opportunity; excluding them, people who had used marijuana remained more likely to start cocaine once offered (adjusted relative risk 20.4, 95% CI 10.2 to 40.7).
key_findings.locator: Results › Do these observed findings depend on seeking out cocaine exposure opportunities?, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2, part C (p. 922)

key_findings.finding: Lifetime status at interview (not time-ordered): marijuana use in 28.4% of 12- to 18-year-olds who had used alcohol or tobacco against 0.6% of those who had not (crude odds ratio 63.8, 95% CI 51.2 to 79.5); cocaine use in 28.6% of 12- to 25-year-olds who had used marijuana against 0.4% (100.8, 84.4 to 120.3), and in 16.4% after alcohol or tobacco against 0.9% (20.9, 18.2 to 23.9).
key_findings.note: Editors' recomputation from the printed counts reproduces these as crude, unweighted odds ratios.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: reorganizing cross-sectional data into sequences invites bias; the household frame misses the most heavily involved; reports may differ in completeness between people who did and did not use drugs, with no gold standard for either age; and excluding same-year transitions also removed people who accepted an unbidden offer at once under peer pressure.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says an estimated three in four people who had used alcohol or tobacco had had a chance to try marijuana by 18, but on Fig. 1A their curve ends at about 70% (read from a 300-dpi crop), clearly below the 75% line.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite about 70% (or about seven in ten) from the figure, against about one in four for people who had not used alcohol or tobacco.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the race/ethnicity rows add up to 44,660 respondents (41,061 without cocaine use), against 44,624 (41,025) in every other block of the same table (editors' sums).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor (36 respondents); one race/ethnicity cell is misprinted. The race/ethnicity odds ratios are consistent with their own rows.

reporting_issues.issue: Several relative risks are printed only as approximate multiples (about three, about seven, 15) with intervals to one decimal, and the text does not always say whether an estimate comes from the adjusted model.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should cite the interval or say 'about'; the exact point estimates cannot be recovered from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Exclusions for missing answers and the number of respondents censored at tied ages are not reported. The 12- to 18-year-olds number 26,015 in Table 1 but 25,916 in the age rows of Table 2 (editors' sum), with more 12- to 14-year-olds in Table 2 (11,655 against 11,641) and fewer at 15 (3,740 against 3,760) and 16–18 (10,521 against 10,614).
reporting_issues.consequence: Losses to missing data and ties are unknown; censoring at ties removes people whose earlier and later events fell in the same year, which could bias the estimates in either direction.

reporting_issues.issue: The surveys use a multistage area-probability design, but no sampling weights or design-based variance estimation is described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The estimates describe the respondents rather than the US population, and the confidence intervals may be too narrow.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Am J Epidemiol 155(10), pp. 918–925 (all pages; Tables 1–2 and Figs. 1–2 checked on rendered pages, figure values read from 300-dpi crops; the appendix tables offered on request or on the authors' website were not available)
